newsitem.title: USA: Rwanda genocide suspect held in Texas jail.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide suspect held in Texas jail.

text.p: A man wanted in Rwanda for genocide was ordered held without bail on Friday after he was arrested by FBI agents in Texas on Thursday.

Elsaphane Ntakirutimana, 73, appeared before U.S. Magistrate Marcel Notzon, who read the charges against him and said he must stay in the Webb County Jail until next Friday when a hearing on whether to set bail would be held.
Ntakirutimana has been charged by the U.N. International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda with genocide, complicity in genocide, conspiracy to commit genocide and crimes against humanity.
The tribunal was set up to try leaders of a wave of ethnic cleansing killings between Hutu and Tutsi tribes in the central African country in 1994. A million people died in the violence.

Ntakirutimana, a Hutu and former Seventh Day Adventist priest in Kibuye, western Rwanda, is accused of telling Tutsis fleeing attacks to take refuge in Mugonero hospital, then participating in a day-long attack April 16, 1994, in which hundreds of men, women and children were killed.
FBI spokesman Mike Appleby said it was likely Ntakirutimana's extradition would be sought, which would require presentation of the evidence against him.
Prosecutors told reporters evidence included statements from a Dutch policeman and a prosecutor with the tribunal.
Ntakirutimana was arrested by the FBI on a highway outside Laredo, which is on the U.S.-Mexico border, as he and his family drove north toward San Antonio, Texas for a vacation.
FBI agents said they had had him under surveillance in Laredo, where he had worked in a health food store for about six months. One of his sons is a Laredo doctor.
A spokeswoman for the U.N. tribunal said on Friday in Tanzania it had been hoped other suspects would be arrested with Ntakirutimana, but that they had apparently escaped.

Ntakirutimana's family told reporters outside the hearing that he was in bad health with unspecified problems of the oesophagus and could die in jail. Notzon ordered the U.S. Marshal Service to ensure proper medical attention.
Son John Ntakirutimana said the charges against his father were false and arose out of jealousy that he had maintained good relations with both Hutus and Tutsis during the violence.
His father's only crime was that he had attempted to give people refuge at his church, he said.
